page: Amazon Web Services c8gb.24xlarge is a compute-optimized server instance powered by the Nitro hypervisor and custom AWS Graviton ARMv9 Neoverse-V2 processors. It features 96 dedicated physical cores and 96 vCPUs running at 2.8 GHz, with no simultaneous multithreading. The system is equipped with 192.0 GB of system memory, providing a resource density of 2.0 GB per core. It lacks local storage and dedicated GPU hardware, relying entirely on network-attached storage and network-based resources. Network connectivity is supported by a 200 Gbps baseline bandwidth.

Benchmark data indicates top-tier multi-core performance, with stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression scores all placing in the top 10% of tested systems. Memory bandwidth is exceptionally high, with cached read-only speeds reaching 11,075.0 GB/sec and uncached large-block reads at 480.77 GB/sec. Single-core performance is moderate, with stress-ng single-core scoring in the middle 50% and Geekbench single-core in the top 25%. The instance excels in parallelized tasks, showing top-tier results in software compilation, ray tracing, Redis SET operations, and static web serving throughput.

The c8gb.24xlarge offers high compute density and memory bandwidth efficiency typical of the ARMv9 architecture, making it highly cost-efficient for highly parallelized workloads. However, tradeoffs include the complete absence of local storage, requiring reliance on network-attached storage, and the lack of a GPU, which limits its utility for heavy graphics or non-CPU-bound machine learning tasks. Additionally, the arm64 architecture requires software compiled specifically for ARM processors. The 2.0 GB of RAM per core ratio also makes it less suitable for memory-intensive databases compared to memory-optimized instances.

This instance is highly suited for compute-intensive, highly parallel workloads. Appropriate applications include large-scale software compilation, multi-threaded data decompression, high-throughput static web serving, Redis in-memory caching, and CPU-based LLM text generation.
